claim: The potassium channel subunit KV1.8 (Kcna10) is essential for the distinctive outwardly rectifying conductances of type I and II vestibular hair cells.
source: The potassium channel subunit KV1.8 (Kcna10) is essential for the distinctive outwardly rectifying conductances of type I and II vestibular hair cells
evidence: This is the title claim, supported by experimental data showing elimination of gK,L in type I cells and gA/gDR in type II cells upon KV1.8 knockout.

claim: Mature type I HCs express a large and very unusual potassium conductance, gK,L, which activates negative to resting potential.
source: Mature type I HCs express a large and very unusual potassium conductance, gK,L, which activates negative to resting potential, confers very negative resting potentials and low input resistances, and enhances an unusual non-quantal transmission from type I cells onto their calyceal afferent terminals.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by voltage clamp data showing activation at negative potentials.

claim: gK,L confers very negative resting potentials and low input resistances in type I HCs.
source: Mature type I HCs express a large and very unusual potassium conductance, gK,L, which activates negative to resting potential, confers very negative resting potentials and low input resistances, and enhances an unusual non-quantal transmission from type I cells onto their calyceal afferent terminals.
evidence: Supported by current clamp measurements showing Vrest ~-87 mV and Rin ~50 MΩ in controls vs -63 mV and 1400 MΩ in knockouts.

claim: gK,L enhances an unusual non-quantal transmission from type I cells onto their calyceal afferent terminals.
source: Mature type I HCs express a large and very unusual potassium conductance, gK,L, which activates negative to resting potential, confers very negative resting potentials and low input resistances, and enhances an unusual non-quantal transmission from type I cells onto their calyceal afferent terminals.
evidence: Cited from previous work (Contini et al., 2012; Contini et al., 2017; Contini et al., 2020; Govindaraju et al., 2023).

claim: KV1.8 is necessary for gK,L in type I HCs.
source: We found that KV1.8 is necessary not just for gK,L but also for fast-inactivating and delayed rectifier currents in type II HCs, which activate positive to resting potential.
evidence: Demonstrated by elimination of gK,L in Kcna10-/- type I HCs as shown in voltage clamp experiments.

claim: KV1.8 is necessary for fast-inactivating and delayed rectifier currents in type II HCs.
source: We found that KV1.8 is necessary not just for gK,L but also for fast-inactivating and delayed rectifier currents in type II HCs, which activate positive to resting potential.
evidence: Shown by elimination of gA and reduction of gDR in Kcna10-/- type II HCs.

claim: The distinct properties of the three KV1.8-dependent conductances may reflect different mixing with other KV subunits that are differentially expressed in type I and II HCs.
source: The distinct properties of the three KV1.8-dependent conductances may reflect different mixing with other KV subunits that are reported to be differentially expressed in type I and II HCs.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on known differential expression patterns and the different biophysical properties observed.

claim: In KV1.8-null HCs of both types, residual outwardly rectifying conductances include KV7 (Knq) channels.
source: In KV1.8-null HCs of both types, residual outwardly rectifying conductances include KV7 (Knq) channels.
evidence: Demonstrated by XE991 sensitivity of residual currents in knockout HCs.

claim: In both HC types, KV1.8-dependent conductances increase the speed and damping of voltage responses.
source: Current clamp records show that in both HC types, KV1.8-dependent conductances increase the speed and damping of voltage responses.
evidence: Shown by current clamp experiments comparing control and knockout HCs.

claim: Features that speed up vestibular receptor potentials and non-quantal afferent transmission may have helped stabilize locomotion as tetrapods moved from water to land.
source: Features that speed up vestibular receptor potentials and non-quantal afferent transmission may have helped stabilize locomotion as tetrapods moved from water to land.
evidence: This is an evolutionary speculation based on the functional properties observed.

claim: Type I HCs occur only in amniote vestibular organs.
source: Type I HCs occur only in amniote vestibular organs.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field.

claim: Type I HCs are enveloped by a calyceal afferent terminal.
source: Their most distinctive features are that they are enveloped by a calyceal afferent terminal (Wersall, 1956; Lysakowski and Goldberg, 2004)
evidence: Cited from previous anatomical studies.

claim: gK,L has an activation range from –100 to –60 mV.
source: a large non-inactivating conductance with an activation range from –100 to –60 mV, far more negative than other 'low-voltage-activated' KV channels.
evidence: This is stated based on previous characterization and confirmed by G-V curves in the current study.

claim: gK,L strongly attenuates and speeds up the receptor potentials of type I HCs.
source: gK,L is unusually large and unusually negatively activated, and therefore strongly attenuates and speeds up the receptor potentials of type I HCs (Correia et al., 1996; Rüsch and Eatock, 1996b).
evidence: Cited from previous studies and supported by current clamp data in this study.

claim: gK,L augments non-quantal transmission from type I HC to afferent calyx by providing open channels for K+ flow into the synaptic cleft.
source: In addition, gK,L augments non-quantal transmission from type I HC to afferent calyx by providing open channels for K+ flow into the synaptic cleft (Contini et al., 2012; Contini et al., 2017; Contini et al., 2020; Govindaraju et al., 2023), increasing the speed and linearity of the transmitted signal (Songer and Eatock, 2013).
evidence: Cited from previous mechanistic studies.

claim: Type II HCs have compact afferent synaptic contacts (boutons) where the receptor potential drives quantal release of glutamate.
source: Type II HCs have compact afferent synaptic contacts (boutons) where the receptor potential drives quantal release of glutamate.
evidence: This is established knowledge about type II HC synaptic transmission.

claim: Type II HCs have fast-inactivating (A-type, gA) and delayed rectifier (gDR) conductances that are opened by depolarization above resting potential.
source: They have fast-inactivating (A-type, gA) and delayed rectifier (gDR) conductances that are opened by depolarization above resting potential (Vrest).
evidence: This is established knowledge confirmed by voltage clamp data in this study.

claim: gK,L has been proposed to include 'M-like' KV channels in the KV7 and/or erg channel families.
source: gK,L has been proposed to include 'M-like' KV channels in the KV7 and/or erg channel families (Kharkovets et al., 2000; Hurley et al., 2006; Holt et al., 2007).
evidence: Cited from previous hypotheses in the literature.

claim: KV7.4 was eliminated as a gK,L subunit by experiments on KV7.4-null mice.
source: The KV7.4 subunit was of particular interest because it contributes to the low-voltage-activated conductance, gK,n, in cochlear outer HCs, but was eventually eliminated as a gK,L subunit by experiments on KV7.4-null mice (Spitzmaul et al., 2013).
evidence: Cited from a previous knockout study.

claim: KV1.8 is highly expressed in vestibular sensory epithelia.
source: KV1.8 is highly expressed in vestibular sensory epithelia (Carlisle et al., 2012), particularly HCs (Lee et al., 2013; Scheffer et al., 2015; McInturff et al., 2018), with slight expression elsewhere (skeletal muscle, Lee et al., 2013; kidney, Yao et al., 2002).
evidence: Cited from multiple expression studies.

claim: Kcna10–/– mice show absent or delayed vestibular-evoked potentials.
source: Kcna10–/– mice show absent or delayed vestibular-evoked potentials, the synchronized activity of afferent nerve fibers sensitive to fast linear head motions (Lee et al., 2013).
evidence: Cited from the original knockout mouse characterization.

claim: KV1.8 has a cyclic nucleotide-binding domain.
source: Unique among KV1 channels, KV1.8 has a cyclic nucleotide-binding domain (Lang et al., 2000) with the potential to explain gK,L's known cGMP dependence (Behrend et al., 1997; Chen and Eatock, 2000).
evidence: Cited from molecular characterization studies.

claim: gK,L has known cGMP dependence.
source: Unique among KV1 channels, KV1.8 has a cyclic nucleotide-binding domain (Lang et al., 2000) with the potential to explain gK,L's known cGMP dependence (Behrend et al., 1997; Chen and Eatock, 2000).
evidence: Cited from previous functional studies.

claim: KV1.8 expression is necessary for gK,L in type I HCs.
source: Our comparison of whole-cell currents and immunohistochemistry in type I HCs from Kcna10–/– and Kcna10+/+,+/– mouse utricles showed that KV1.8 expression is necessary for gK,L.
evidence: Demonstrated by elimination of gK,L in knockout mice.

claim: KV1.8 expression is required for A-type and delayed rectifier conductances of type II HCs.
source: More surprisingly, KV1.8 expression is also required for A-type and delayed rectifier conductances of type II HCs.
evidence: Shown by elimination/reduction of these currents in knockout type II HCs.

claim: Eliminating the KV1.8-dependent major conductances revealed a smaller delayed rectifier conductance involving KV7 channels in both HC types.
source: In both HC types, eliminating the KV1.8-dependent major conductances revealed a smaller delayed rectifier conductance involving KV7 channels.
evidence: Demonstrated by XE991 sensitivity of residual currents.

claim: Recordings are from 412 type I and II HCs from mice between postnatal day (P) 5 and P370.
source: Recordings are from 412 type I and II HCs (53% LES, 30% MES, 17% striola) from mice between postnatal day (P) 5 and P370.
evidence: This describes the dataset used in the study.

claim: Above P18, there were no substantial changes in KV channel properties.
source: Above P18, we did not see substantial changes in KV channel properties, as reported (González-Garrido et al., 2021).
evidence: Based on analysis of age-dependent data and cited previous work.

claim: Kcna10–/– animals appeared to be healthy and to develop and age normally.
source: Kcna10–/– animals appeared to be healthy and to develop and age normally, as reported (Lee et al., 2013), and HCs were healthy (see Methods for criteria).
evidence: Observational data from the current study and cited previous report.

claim: In Kcna10+/+,+/– type I HCs, gK,L produces distinctive whole-cell current responses to voltage steps.
source: The large low-voltage-activated conductance, gK,L, in Kcna10+/+,+/– type I HCs produces distinctive whole-cell current responses to voltage steps, as highlighted by our standard type I voltage protocol (Figure 1A).
evidence: Shown in voltage clamp recordings in Figure 1A.

claim: A large transient inward current is a hallmark of gK,L.
source: We use the large transient inward current as a hallmark of gK,L.
evidence: This is a defining characteristic used for identification, shown in Figure 1A.

claim: No difference was detected between the Boltzmann parameters of gK,L G–V curves from Kcna10+/– and Kcna10+/+ type I HCs.
source: We detected no difference between the Boltzmann parameters of gK,L G–V curves from Kcna10+/– and Kcna10+/+ type I HCs.
evidence: Statistical comparison of G-V parameters between genotypes.

claim: Kcna10–/– type I HCs produced no inward transient current at the step from holding potential to –124 mV.
source: For a similar voltage protocol, Kcna10–/– type I HCs (Figure 1B) produced no inward transient current at the step from holding potential to –124 mV and much smaller depolarization-activated currents during the iterated steps, even at much more positive potentials.
evidence: Shown in voltage clamp recordings in Figure 1B.

claim: The maximal conductance of Kcna10–/– type I HCs was over 10-fold smaller than controls.
source: the maximal conductance (gmax) of the Kcna10–/– HC was over 10-fold smaller (Figure 1C.1)
evidence: Quantified from G-V curves shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The G-V curve of Kcna10–/– type I HCs was positively shifted by >40 mV compared to controls.
source: and the curve was positively shifted by >40 mV (Figure 1C.2).
evidence: Measured from Boltzmann fits to G-V data in Figure 1C.

claim: In type I HCs from Kcna10+/+,+/– mice, the G–V parameters of outwardly rectifying currents transitioned over the first 15–20 postnatal days from values for a conventional delayed rectifier to gK,L values.
source: In type I HCs from Kcna10+/+,+,– mice, the G–V parameters of outwardly rectifying currents transitioned over the first 15–20 postnatal days from values for a conventional delayed rectifier, activating positive to resting potential, to gK,L values (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A), as previously described (Rüsch et al., 1998; Géléoc et al., 2004; Hurley et al., 2006).
evidence: Shown in developmental analysis in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A and cited from previous studies.

claim: No effects of KV1.8 deletion were seen in the delayed rectifier currents of immature type I HCs.
source: No effects of KV1.8 deletion were seen in the delayed rectifier currents of immature type I HCs (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B), showing that they were not immature forms of the KV1.8-dependent gK,L channels.
evidence: Comparison of conductance density in young HCs between genotypes shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Kcna10–/– type I HCs had a much smaller residual delayed rectifier that activated positive to resting potential, with Vhalf ~–40 mV and gmax density of 1.3 nS/pF.
source: Kcna10–/– type I HCs had a much smaller residual delayed rectifier that activated positive to resting potential, with Vhalf ~–40 mV and gmax density of 1.3 nS/pF.
evidence: Measured from G-V analysis of knockout type I HCs.

claim: Type I HCs from Kcna10–/– animals had smaller membrane capacitances (4–5 pF) than Kcna10+/– (6 pF) and Kcna10+/+ (6–7 pF) type I HCs.
source: While the cells of Kcna10–/– and Kcna10+/– epithelia appeared healthy, type I HCs had smaller membrane capacitances (Cm): 4–5 pF in Kcna10–/– type I HCs, ~20% smaller than Kcna10+/– type I HCs (~6 pF) and ~30% smaller than Kcna10+/+ type I HCs (6–7 pF; Table 2).
evidence: Measured capacitance values reported in Table 2.

claim: The lack of change in soma sizes by deletion of KV1.8 suggests that surface area was not different.
source: While Cm scales with surface area, the lack of change in soma sizes by deletion of KV1.8 (Supplementary file 1b) suggests that surface area was not different.
evidence: Inference from morphological measurements in Supplementary file 1b.

claim: In Kcna10–/– type I HCs, Vrest was much less negative than in controls.
source: In Kcna10–/– type I HCs, Vrest was much less negative (Figure 2A.1)
evidence: Measured resting potentials shown in Figure 2A.1.

claim: In Kcna10–/– type I HCs, Rin was greater by ~20-fold than in controls.
source: Rin was greater by ~20-fold (Figure 2A.2)
evidence: Measured input resistance shown in Figure 2A.2.

claim: In Kcna10–/– type I HCs, membrane charging times were commensurately longer than in controls.
source: and membrane charging times were commensurately longer (Figure 2A.3).
evidence: Measured time constants shown in Figure 2A.3.

claim: The large K+-selective conductance at Vrest holds Vrest close to EK and minimizes gain (ΔV/ΔI) in type I HCs.
source: The large K+-selective conductance at Vrest holds Vrest close to EK (K+ equilibrium potential) and minimizes gain (ΔV/ΔI), such that voltage-gated conductances are negligibly affected by the input current and the cell produces approximately linear, static responses to iterated current steps.
evidence: This is an inference from the biophysical properties of gK,L and observed current clamp responses.

claim: With KV1.8 (gK,L), the voltage response of the type I HC is smaller but better reproduces the time course of the input current.
source: Overall, comparison of the Kcna10+/+,+/– and Kcna10–/– responses shows that with KV1.8 (gK,L), the voltage response of the type I HC is smaller but better reproduces the time course of the input current.
evidence: Conclusion from current clamp experiments comparing genotypes.

claim: Most (81/84) Kcna10+/+,+/– type II HCs expressed a rapidly activating, rapidly inactivating A-type conductance (gA).
source: Most (81/84) Kcna10+/+,+/– type II HCs expressed a rapidly activating, rapidly inactivating A-type conductance (gA).
evidence: Quantification of cells expressing gA in control animals.

claim: A current is defined as the outwardly rectifying current that inactivates by over 30% within 200 ms.
source: We define A current as the outwardly rectifying current that inactivates by over 30% within 200 ms.
evidence: This is the operational definition used in the study.

claim: gA was more prominent in extrastriolar zones.
source: gA was more prominent in extrastriolar zones, as reported (Holt et al., 1999; Weng and Correia, 1999).
evidence: Observed zonal differences confirmed by previous reports.

claim: Fast inactivation was a larger fraction of the total inactivation in LES than striola (~0.5 vs 0.3).
source: and fast inactivation was a larger fraction of the total inactivation in LES than striola (~0.5 vs 0.3, Figure 3A.4).
evidence: Quantified from fits and shown in Figure 3A.4.

claim: Kcna10+/– HCs had smaller currents than Kcna10+/+ HCs, reflecting a smaller gDR.
source: Kcna10+/– HCs had smaller currents than Kcna10+/+ HCs, reflecting a smaller gDR (Figure 3D)
evidence: Shown in G-V curves in Figure 3D demonstrating gene dosage effect.

claim: Kcna10+/– HCs had faster fast inactivation than Kcna10+/+ HCs.
source: and faster fast inactivation (Figure 3A.3).
evidence: Statistical comparison shown in Figure 3A.3.

claim: For Kcna10+/+ and Kcna10+/– HCs, the voltage dependence as summarized by Vhalf and slope factor (S) was similar.
source: For Kcna10+/+ and Kcna10+/– HCs, the voltage dependence as summarized by Vhalf and slope factor (S) was similar.
evidence: Statistical comparison of Boltzmann parameters between these genotypes.

claim: Relative to gSS, gPeak had a more positive Vhalf (~–21 vs ~–26) and greater S (~12 vs ~9).
source: Relative to gSS, gPeak had a more positive Vhalf (~–21 vs ~–26) and greater S (~12 vs ~9, Figure 3D, Table 4).
evidence: Comparison of Boltzmann parameters for peak vs steady-state conductances.

claim: Only gPeak showed zonal variation, with more positive Vhalf in LES than striola (~–20 vs ~–24 mV).
source: Only gPeak showed zonal variation, with more positive Vhalf in LES than striola (~–20 vs ~–24 mV, Figure 3D, Table 4).
evidence: Statistical comparison across zones for peak conductance.

claim: Kcna10–/– type II HCs from all zones were missing gA and 30–50% of gDR.
source: Kcna10–/– type II HCs from all zones were missing gA and 30–50% of gDR (Figure 3B–D).
evidence: Shown by comparison of currents and G-V curves in Figure 3B-D.

claim: The residual delayed rectifier in Kcna10–/– type II HCs (1.3 nS/pF) had a more positive Vhalf than gDR in Kcna10+/+,+/– HCs (~–20 vs ~–26 mV).
source: The residual delayed rectifier (1.3 nS/pF) had a more positive Vhalf than gDR in Kcna10+/+,+/– HCs (~–20 vs ~–26 mV, Figure 3D.2).
evidence: Comparison of Boltzmann parameters shown in Figure 3D.2.

claim: In Kcna10+/+,+/– type II HCs, gA was present at all ages with a higher % inactivation after P18 than at P5–P10.
source: In Kcna10+/+,+/– type II HCs, gA was present at all ages with a higher % inactivation after P18 than at P5–P10 (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A.4).
evidence: Developmental analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2A.4.

claim: Small rapidly inactivating outward currents were seen in a minority of Kcna10–/– type II HCs (23%, 7/30), all >P12 and extrastriolar.
source: We saw small rapidly inactivating outward currents in a minority of Kcna10–/– type II HCs (23%, 7/30), all >P12 and extrastriolar (Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Quantification of cells with residual fast-inactivating currents.

claim: In type II HCs, absence of KV1.8 did not change Vrest.
source: In type II HCs, absence of KV1.8 did not change Vrest (Figure 4A.1)
evidence: Comparison of resting potentials shown in Figure 4A.1.

claim: Absence of KV1.8 increased the incidence of sharp electrical resonance in type II HCs.
source: Absence of KV1.8 increased the incidence of sharp electrical resonance in type II HCs.
evidence: Shown by increased quality factor (Qe) in knockout cells.

claim: Median resonance quality (Qe) was greater in Kcna10–/– (1.33) than Kcna10+/+ (0.66) or Kcna10+/– (0.59) type II HCs.
source: Median resonance quality (Qe, sharpness of tuning) was greater in Kcna10–/– (1.33, n=26) than Kcna10+/+ (0.66, n = 23) or Kcna10+/– (0.59, n = 44) type II HCs.
evidence: Quantification of resonance quality from fits to voltage responses.

claim: KV1.8 immunoreactivity was present along the basolateral membranes of both HC types in Kcna10+/+ utricles.
source: Figure 5 compares KV1.8 immunoreactivity in Kcna10+/+ and Kcna10–/– utricles, showing specific immunoreactivity along the basolateral membranes of both HC types in Kcna10+/+ utricles.
evidence: Immunohistochemistry shown in Figure 5.

claim: KV1.8 immunoreactivity was present in HC membrane apposing KV7.4-stained calyx inner face in Kcna10+/+ utricles and not in Kcna10–/– utricles.
source: KV1.8 immunoreactivity was present in HC membrane apposing KV7.4-stained calyx inner face in Kcna10+/+ utricles (Figure 5A.1 and A.2) and not in Kcna10–/– utricles (Figure 5A.3).
evidence: Immunohistochemistry comparison shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Comparison of control and null tissue showed selective expression of KV1.8 in HC membranes, and that some supporting cell staining is non-specific.
source: Here, comparison of control and null tissue showed selective expression of HC membranes, and that some supporting cell staining is non-specific.
evidence: Conclusion from immunohistochemistry comparing genotypes.

claim: KV1.8, like most KV1 subunits, does not show fast inactivation as a heterologously expressed homomer.
source: KV1.8, like most KV1 subunits, does not show fast inactivation as a heterologously expressed homomer (Lang et al., 2000; Ranjan et al., 2019; Dierich et al., 2020)
evidence: Cited from heterologous expression studies.

claim: KV1.8-dependent channels in type I HCs do not show fast inactivation.
source: nor do the KV1.8-dependent channels in type I HCs, as we show, and in cochlear inner HCs (Dierich et al., 2020).
evidence: Shown by lack of inactivation in gK,L and cited for cochlear cells.

claim: KVβ1 (Kcnb1) is present in type II HCs alongside KVβ2 (Kcnb2).
source: KVβ1 (Kcnb1) is present in type II HCs alongside KVβ2 (Kcnb2) (McInturff et al., 2018; Jan et al., 2021; Orvis et al., 2021)
evidence: Cited from expression studies.

claim: KVβ2 does not confer rapid inactivation.
source: which does not confer rapid inactivation (Dwenger et al., 2022).
evidence: Cited from functional characterization.

claim: KV1.4 is the only KV1 subunit which, when expressed as a homomer, has complete N-type (fast) inactivation.
source: Another possibility is that in type II HCs, KV1.8 subunits heteromultimerize with KV1.4 subunits—the only KV1 subunits which, when expressed as a homomer, have complete N-type (fast) inactivation (Stühmer et al., 1989).
evidence: Cited from characterization of KV1.4.

claim: KV1.4 has been linked to gA in pigeon type II HCs.
source: KV1.4 has been linked to gA in pigeon type II HCs (Correia et al., 2008)
evidence: Cited from previous work in avian vestibular system.

claim: KV1.4 is the second-most abundant KV1 transcript in mammalian vestibular HCs, after KV1.8.
source: and is the second-most abundant KV1 transcript in mammalian vestibular HCs, after KV1.8 (Scheffer et al., 2015).
evidence: Cited from transcriptomic analysis.

claim: KV1.4 is expressed in type II HCs but not type I HCs.
source: KV1.4 is expressed in type II HCs but not type I HCs (McInturff et al., 2018; Orvis et al., 2021)
evidence: Cited from single-cell expression studies.

claim: KV1.4 is not found in striolar HCs.
source: and is not found in striolar HCs (Jan et al., 2021; Orvis et al., 2021)
evidence: Cited from expression studies showing zonal differences.

claim: In Kcna10–/– HCs, absence of IK,L and IA revealed smaller delayed rectifier K+ currents that activated positive to resting potential and lacked fast inactivation.
source: In Kcna10–/– HCs, absence of IK,L and IA revealed smaller delayed rectifier K+ currents that, unlike IK,L, activated positive to resting potential and, unlike IA, lacked fast inactivation.
evidence: Characterization of residual currents in knockout cells.

claim: 10 µM XE991 blocked about half of the residual KV conductance in Kcna10–/– HCs of both types.
source: In Kcna10–/– HCs of both types, 10 µM XE991 blocked about half of the residual KV conductance (Figure 7B.1)
evidence: Pharmacological experiment shown in Figure 7B.1.

claim: The XE991-sensitive conductance did not inactivate substantially within 200 ms at any voltage, consistent with KV7.2, 7.3, 7.4, and 7.5 currents.
source: In all tested HCs (P8–355, median P224), the XE991-sensitive conductance did not inactivate substantially within 200 ms at any voltage, consistent with KV7.2, 7.3, 7.4, and 7.5 currents (Wang, 1998; Kubisch et al., 1999; Schroeder et al., 2000; Jensen et al., 2007; Xu et al., 2007).
evidence: Kinetic analysis of XE991-sensitive current compared to known KV7 properties.

claim: The voltage dependence and gmax density of gDR(KV7) were comparable across HC types and genotypes.
source: The voltage dependence and gmax density (gmax/Cm) of gDR(KV7) were comparable across HC types and genotypes (Figure 7B.2–4).
evidence: Statistical comparison shown in Figure 7B.2-4.

claim: KV7.4 has been shown in type I HCs with immunogold labeling.
source: Although KV7.4 was not detectable in HCs during immunostaining (Figure 5), KV7.4 has been shown in type I HCs with immunogold labeling (Kharkovets et al., 2000; Hurley et al., 2006).
evidence: Cited from previous immunogold studies.

claim: XE991 also blocked a small conductance that activated negative to rest in one striolar Kcna10–/– type I HC.
source: In one striolar Kcna10–/– type I HC, XE991 also blocked a small conductance that activated negative to rest (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A, B).
evidence: Single cell example shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: This very negatively activating KV7 conductance (Vhalf ~ = –100 mV) was detected only in Kcna10–/– type I HCs from the striola (5/23 vs 0/45 extrastriolar).
source: This conductance (Vhalf ~ = –100 mV, Figure 7—figure supplement 1C) was detected only in Kcna10–/– type I HCs from the striola (5/23 vs 0/45 extrastriolar).
evidence: Quantification of occurrence across zones shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1C.

claim: BK is expressed in mouse utricular HCs.
source: BK is expressed in mouse utricular HCs (McInturff et al., 2018; Jan et al., 2021; Orvis et al., 2021).
evidence: Cited from expression studies.

claim: Little to no effect of the BK-channel blocker iberiotoxin at 100 nM was found.
source: However, Ca2+-dependent currents have not been observed in mouse utricular HCs, and we found little to no effect of the BK-channel blocker iberiotoxin at a dose (100 nM) well beyond the IC50: percent blocked at –30 mV was 2 ± 6% (3 Kcna10–/– type I HCs); 1 ± 5% (5 Kcna10+/+,+/– type II HCs); 7% and 14% (2 Kcna10–/– type II HCs).
evidence: Pharmacological experiment testing BK contribution.

claim: In type I HCs from both control and null utricles, IH and IKir were less prevalent in striola than extrastriola.
source: In type I HCs from both control and null utricles, IH and IKir were less prevalent in striola than extrastriola, and, when present, the combined inward current was smaller (Figure 7—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Zonal comparison shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2.

claim: KV1.8 is a pore-forming subunit of gK,L, gA, and part of gDR [gDR(KV1.8)].
source: We conclude that KV1.8 is a pore-forming subunit of gK,L, gA, and part of gDR [gDR(KV1.8)].
evidence: Conclusion from knockout experiments and immunolocalization.

claim: Fast inactivation of gA may arise from heteromultimerization of non-inactivating KV1.8 subunits and inactivating KV1.4 subunits.
source: We suggest that fast inactivation of gA may arise from heteromultimerization of non-inactivating KV1.8 subunits and inactivating KV1.4 subunits.
evidence: Proposed mechanism based on expression patterns and biophysical properties.

claim: A substantial component of the residual delayed rectifier current in both type I and II HCs comprises KV7 channels.
source: Finally, we showed that a substantial component of the residual delayed rectifier current in both type I and II HCs comprises KV7 channels.
evidence: Demonstrated by XE991 sensitivity.

claim: KV1.8 is expressed in HCs from mammalian cochlea.
source: KV1.8 is expressed in HCs from mammalian cochlea (Dierich et al., 2020)
evidence: Cited from cochlear studies.

claim: KV1.8 is expressed in avian utricle.
source: avian utricle (Scheibinger et al., 2022)
evidence: Cited from avian studies.

claim: KV1.8 is expressed in zebrafish.
source: and zebrafish (Erickson and Nicolson, 2015).
evidence: Cited from zebrafish studies.

claim: In anamniotes, which lack type I cells and gK,L, KV1.8 contributes to gA and gDR.
source: Our work suggests that in anamniotes, which lack type I cells and gK,L, KV1.8 contributes to gA and gDR, which are widespread in vertebrate HCs (reviewed in Meredith and Rennie, 2016).
evidence: Inference from the current findings and evolutionary considerations.

claim: Recent single-cell expression studies on mouse utricles have detected just one KV1 subunit, KV1.8, in mouse type I HCs.
source: Recent single-cell expression studies on mouse utricles (McInturff et al., 2018; Jan et al., 2021; Orvis et al., 2021) have detected just one KV1 subunit, KV1.8, in mouse type I HCs.
evidence: Cited from single-cell transcriptomic studies.

claim: gK,L channels are present at very high density (~150 per μm2 in rat type I).
source: Given that KV1.8 can only form multimers with KV1 family members, and given that gK,L channels are present at very high density (~150 per μm2 in rat type I, Chen and Eatock, 2000)
evidence: Cited from previous channel density measurements.

claim: Most or all of the gK,L channels are KV1.8 homomers.
source: it stands to reason that most or all of the channels are KV1.8 homomers.
evidence: Inference from expression data and channel density.

claim: gK,L and heterologously expressed KV1.8 homomers in oocytes are non-inactivating and blocked by millimolar Ba2+ and 4-aminopyridine and >10 mM tetraethyl ammonium.
source: gK,L (Rüsch and Eatock, 1996a) and heterologously expressed KV1.8 homomers in oocytes (Lang et al., 2000) are non-inactivating and blocked by millimolar Ba2+ and 4-aminopyridine and >10 mM tetraethyl ammonium.
evidence: Comparison of pharmacological properties from cited studies.

claim: Unlike channels with KV1.1, KV1.2, and KV1.6 subunits, gK,L is not sensitive to 10 nM α-dendrotoxin.
source: Unlike channels with KV1.1, KV1.2, and KV1.6 subunits, gK,L is not sensitive to 10 nM α-dendrotoxin (Rüsch and Eatock, 1996a).
evidence: Cited pharmacological characterization.

claim: gK,L and heterologously expressed KV1.8 channels have similar single-channel conductances (~20 pS for gK,L at positive potentials; 11 pS in oocytes).
source: gK,L and heterologously expressed KV1.8 channels have similar single-channel conductances (~20 pS for gK,L at positive potentials, Chen and Eatock, 2000; 11 pS in oocytes, Lang et al., 2000).
evidence: Comparison of single-channel properties from cited studies.

claim: gK,L is inhibited—or positively voltage-shifted—by cGMP.
source: gK,L is inhibited—or positively voltage-shifted—by cGMP (Behrend et al., 1997; Chen and Eatock, 2000), presumably via the C-terminal cyclic nucleotide-binding domain of KV1.8.
evidence: Cited functional studies and inference about mechanism.

claim: A major novel property of gK,L is that it activates 30–60 mV negative to type II KV1.8 conductances and most other low-voltage-activated KV channels.
source: A major novel property of gK,L is that it activates 30–60 mV negative to type II KV1.8 conductances and most other low-voltage-activated KV channels (Ranjan et al., 2019).
evidence: Comparison of voltage dependence with other channels.

claim: Heterologously expressed homomeric KV1.8 channels have an activation Vhalf of –10 to 0 mV.
source: Heterologously expressed homomeric KV1.8 channels have an activation Vhalf of –10 to 0 mV (X. laevis oocytes, Lang et al., 2000; Chinese hamster ovary cells, Dierich et al., 2020).
evidence: Cited from heterologous expression studies.

claim: In cochlear inner HCs, currents attributed to KV1.8 have a near-zero activation Vhalf (–4 mV).
source: In cochlear inner HCs, currents attributed to KV1.8 (by subtraction of other candidates) have a near-zero activation Vhalf (–4 mV, Dierich et al., 2020).
evidence: Cited from cochlear HC study.

claim: Elevation of extracellular K+ by the enveloping calyceal terminal, unique to type I HCs, may contribute to the negative voltage dependence of gK,L.
source: (1) Elevation of extracellular K+ by the enveloping calyceal terminal, unique to type I HCs (Lim et al., 2011; Contini et al., 2012; Spaiardi et al., 2020; Govindaraju et al., 2023). High K+ increases conductance though gK,L channels (Contini et al., 2020), perhaps through K+-mediated relief of C-type inactivation (López-Barneo et al., 1993; Baukrowitz and Yellen, 1995).
evidence: Proposed mechanism based on cited studies of K+ effects.

claim: gK,L is open at rest even in neonatal mouse utricles cultured without innervation.
source: We note, however, that gK,L is open at rest even in neonatal mouse utricles cultured without innervation (Rüsch et al., 1998) and persists in dissociated type I HCs (Chen and Eatock, 2000; Hurley et al., 2006).
evidence: Cited from culture and dissociation studies.

claim: The high density of gK,L implies close packing of channels, possibly represented by particles (12–14 nm) seen in freeze-fracture electron microscopy of the type I HC membrane.
source: (2) The high density of gK,L (~50 nS/pF in striolar Kcna10+/+ HCs) implies close packing of channels, possibly represented by particles (12–14 nm) seen in freeze-fracture electron microscopy of the type I HC membrane (Gulley and Bagger-Sjöbäck, 1979; Sousa et al., 2009).
evidence: Inference from density measurements and cited EM observations.

claim: Close channel packing might hyperpolarize in situ voltage dependence of gK,L, as proposed for KV7.4 channels in outer HCs.
source: Such close channel packing might hyperpolarize in situ voltage dependence of gK,L, as proposed for KV7.4 channels in outer HCs (Perez-Flores et al., 2020).
evidence: Speculative mechanism based on analogy to cited work.

claim: Type I HCs express ADAM11.
source: Type I HC-specific partners that may facilitate this close packing include ADAM11 (McInturff et al., 2018)
evidence: Cited from expression study.

claim: ADAM11 clusters presynaptic KV1.1 and KV1.2 to enable ephaptic coupling at a cerebellar synapse.
source: which clusters presynaptic KV1.1 and KV1.2 to enable ephaptic coupling at a cerebellar synapse (Kole et al., 2015).
evidence: Cited from cerebellar synapse study.

claim: Type I HCs express KVβ1.
source: (3) Modulation by accessory subunits. Type I HCs express KVβ1 (McInturff et al., 2018; Orvis et al., 2021)
evidence: Cited from expression studies.

claim: KVβ1 can confer fast inactivation and hyperpolarize activation Vhalf by ~10 mV.
source: an accessory subunit that can confer fast inactivation and hyperpolarize activation Vhalf by ~10 mV.
evidence: This is established knowledge about KVβ1 function.

claim: Cochlear inner HCs co-express KV1.8 and KVβ1 but their KV1.8 conductance has a near-0 Vhalf.
source: Arguments against this possibility include that gK,L lacks fast inactivation (Rüsch and Eatock, 1996a; Hurley et al., 2006; Spaiardi et al., 2017) and that cochlear inner HCs co-express KV1.8 and KVβ1 (Liu et al., 2018) but their KV1.8 conductance has a near-0 Vhalf (Dierich et al., 2020).
evidence: Cited from cochlear studies.

claim: Zonal variation in the extent and speed of N-type inactivation might arise from differential expression of KV1.4.
source: Zonal variation in the extent and speed of N-type inactivation (Figure 3A) might arise from differential expression of KV1.4.
evidence: Proposed explanation for zonal differences.

claim: The small fast-inactivating conductance in ~20% of extrastriolar Kcna10–/– type II HCs might flow through KV1.4 homomers.
source: The small fast-inactivating conductance in ~20% of extrastriolar Kcna10–/– type II HCs (Figure 3—figure supplement 3) might flow through KV1.4 homomers.
evidence: Proposed explanation for residual fast-inactivating current.

claim: KVβ1, together with KV1.4, has been linked to gA in pigeon vestibular HCs.
source: Fast inactivation may also receive contribution from KVβ subunits. KVβ1 is expressed in type II HCs (McInturff et al., 2018; Jan et al., 2021; Orvis et al., 2021), and, together with KV1.4, has been linked to gA in pigeon vestibular HCs (Correia et al., 2008).
evidence: Cited from avian study.

claim: KVβ2 accelerates but does not confer fast inactivation.
source: KVβ2, also expressed in type II HCs (McInturff et al., 2018; Orvis et al., 2021), accelerates but does not confer fast inactivation.
evidence: Cited from expression studies and known KVβ2 function.

claim: gA may include heteromers of KV1.8 with other subunits that confer rapid inactivation, while gDR(KV1.8) may comprise homomeric KV1.8 channels.
source: We speculate that gA and gDR(KV1.8) have different subunit composition: gA may include heteromers of KV1.8 with other subunits that confer rapid inactivation, while gDR(KV1.8) may comprise homomeric KV1.8 channels, given that they do not have N-type inactivation.
evidence: Speculative model based on inactivation properties.

claim: In both type I and II utricular HCs, KV1.8-dependent channels strongly shape receptor potentials in ways that promote temporal fidelity rather than electrical tuning.
source: In both type I and II utricular HCs, KV1.8-dependent channels strongly shape receptor potentials in ways that promote temporal fidelity rather than electrical tuning (Lewis, 1988), consistent with the utricle's role in driving reflexes that compensate for head motions as they occur.
evidence: Functional interpretation based on current clamp data and cited work.

claim: gK,L dominates passive membrane properties in mature Kcna10+/+,+/– type I HCs such that Kcna10–/– type I HCs are expected to have receptor potentials with higher amplitudes but lower low-pass corner frequencies.
source: gK,Ldominates passive membrane properties in mature Kcna10+/+,+/– type I HCs such that Kcna10–/– type I HCs are expected to have receptor potentials with higher amplitudes but lower low-pass corner frequencies, closer to those of type II HCs and immature HCs of all types (Correia et al., 1996; Rüsch and Eatock, 1996a; Songer and Eatock, 2013).
evidence: Prediction based on measured passive properties and cited studies.

claim: In Kcna10–/– epithelia, the lack of a large basolateral conductance open at rest is expected to reduce the speed and gain of non-quantal transmission.
source: In Kcna10–/– epithelia, we expect the lack of a large basolateral conductance open at rest to reduce the speed and gain of non-quantal transmission, which depends on K+ ion efflux from the type I HC to change electrical and K+ potentials in the synaptic cleft (Govindaraju et al., 2023).
evidence: Prediction based on understanding of non-quantal transmission mechanism.

claim: For the type I-calyx synapse, having in the HC a large, non-inactivating K+ conductance open across the physiological range of potentials avoids channel gating time and allows for instantaneous changes in current into the cleft and fast afferent signaling.
source: For the type I-calyx synapse, having in the HC a large, non-inactivating K+ conductance open across the physiological range of potentials avoids channel gating time and allows for instantaneous changes in current into the cleft and fast afferent signaling (Pastras et al., 2023).
evidence: Functional interpretation with cited support.

claim: Adult type II HCs acquire type I-like properties upon deletion of the transcription factor Sox2.
source: Type I and II vestibular HCs are closely related, such that adult type II HCs acquire type I-like properties upon deletion of the transcription factor Sox2 (Stone et al., 2021).
evidence: Cited from genetic manipulation study.

claim: In normal development of the two cell types, the Kcna10 gene generates biophysically distinct and functionally different ion channels.
source: In normal development of the two cell types, the Kcna10 gene generates biophysically distinct and functionally different ion channels, presenting a natural experiment in functional differentiation of sensory receptor cells.
evidence: Summary conclusion from the study's findings.
